- D04 (I.C Background, the proposal and its date) [c1]: "for the CWAFs test procedure in the Federal Register on February 25, 2022, which proposed amendments to the existing test procedure for TE as well as a new test procedure"
- D04 (I.C Background, what it proposed) [c1]: "proposed a new metric, TE2, that captured those aspects of CWAF energy use"
- D02 (II.B Background, standards by manufacture date) [c1]: "for gas-fired CWAFs manufactured starting on January 1, 1994, until January 1, 2023, TE at the maximum rated capacity (i.e., rated maximum input) must be not less than 80 percent"
- D02 (II.B Background, the later level) [c1]: "For gas-fired CWAFs manufactured starting on January 1, 2023, the TE at the maximum rated capacity must be not less than 81 percent."
- D04 (II Discussion, DOE's example) [c1]: "a CWAF with a TE of 81 percent as measured by the amended industry test procedure could, depending on jacket losses and part-load operation, have an actual range of efficiencies from 77.5 to 82 percent using the appendix B test procedure for TE2"
- D04 (II.C, jacket losses) [c1]: "could account for as much as a 2.5 percent difference in efficiency"
- D04 (II.C, weighting DOE adopted) [c1]: "adopted the 50 percent weighting at full load and part load"
- D04 (II.C, NEEA's modeling) [c1]: "to operating as little as 25 percent of the time at full load (and 75 percent at part load)"

sections.lever checks:
- Family and target: h1, sketch i01. A derived TE2 figure for a furnace whose federal minimum is not the 81
  percent of DOE's printed example, with the part-load piece re-weighted at NEEA's largest modeled share.
  Target medium (user, 2026-10-10: no Easy slot on this bundle, "target medium and high").
- History: rev 0 said "built in 2022"; its removal probe without Doc 2 forced the gold by recalling the
  January 1, 2023 compliance date (p 0.65). Rev 1 dated the furnace by Doc 2's own publication ("DOE
  published a final determination not to amend ... standards ... built that day") and was measured: Run 1,
  "In band - Easy tier", Low 3/5, both documents needed. Rev 2 keeps the gold, inputs and ticked documents and
  changes only the date anchor.
- What Run 1 showed (rev 1, Version 6f4ab4, raw verdicts/AQ-02770_difficulty_2026-10-11_1119.txt): all five
  low attempts did the re-weighting (2.5 + 1.5 = 4.0), so that step separated no one. Three opened Doc 2
  because the question's first sentence named its determination, read "published December 23, 2022" and
  the "until January 1, 2023" rule side by side, and took 80. Two took 81 and answered 77.0: attempt 2 saw
  both dates and chose 81 because "the base TE they used for range example is 81"; attempt 3 took Doc 4 as
  the final determination ("published Jan 17, 2025"). The high model reached 76.0 with every document, 77.0
  twice without Doc 2 (81 inferred from "went from 80 to 81 percent", no recall of the compliance date) and
  76.5 twice without Doc 4. Closed-book 78.7%.
- Repair in rev 2 (one change, the anchor): the tied anchor sent solvers into the document that holds the
  date rule. Rev 2 dates the furnace by an event the TE2 documents report, the day DOE published its
  proposal to create TE2 (February 25, 2022: D04 l.102, D03 l.104, also D02 l.168), so nothing in the
  question leads to Doc 2's standards-by-date sentences. A solver has to ask on its own which minimum
  applied in February 2022; the TE2 documents print only the 81 example and "from 80 to 81 percent".
  Cost, stated plainly: the date is no longer Doc 2-only, so a solver without Doc 2 that recalls the
  January 1, 2023 compliance date reaches the gold (the rev 0 probe's forced guess). Run 1's two
  without-Doc-2 attempts did not use recall, but they were not asked about a 2022 date.
- Dependency plan: D04 l.102 (proposal published February 25, 2022). D02 l.135 (80 percent until January 1,
  2023) and l.136 (81 from that date) -> base 80. D04 l.143 (81 gives 77.5 to 82), l.189 (jacket losses
  2.5), l.187 (50 percent weighting; NEEA 25 percent full load, 75 percent part load). Operations:
  81 - 77.5 - 2.5 = 1; 75 / 50 = 1.5 (times that 1); 80 - 2.5 - 1.5 = 76.0.
- Universe: not applicable (one derived value, no list).
- Necessity: D02 is the only document that dates the 81 percent level (D03 l.144 and D04 l.184 say the gas
  minimum "went from 80 to 81 percent" undated; D01 covers consumer AFUE classes; D05-D07 print no CWAF
  standard). D04 is the only document with NEEA's modeled shares; Run 1 measured both as needed on rev 1,
  and Doc 4's role is unchanged. D03 stays unticked: D04 alone yields its figures. The "or..." box is not
  used anywhere (aq-02147: the check left out one twin and solved from the other), which is also why the
  no-what-if alternate q03 (second source "Doc 3 or Doc 4") is dropped.
- Selected-lever checks: right edition: the 81 percent level is the later edition of the same standard and
  fails "built ... on the day DOE published its proposal to create TE2" (February 25, 2022, before January 1,
  2023). Look-alike events, all after January 1, 2023 and all leading to 81: the June 2, 2023 final rule that

sections.question: For a gas-fired commercial warm air furnace built at the federal minimum thermal efficiency on the day DOE published its proposal to create TE2, how low could TE2 be by DOE's estimates if part load were weighted at the largest share of operating time NEEA's modeling gave it? Give one decimal place.
sections.reasoning:
Step 1. Source input (Doc 4, Background): DOE published its notice of proposed rulemaking for the test procedure, the proposal that created the TE2 metric, in the Federal Register on February 25, 2022.

Step 2. Source input (Doc 2, Background): gas-fired commercial warm air furnaces manufactured before January 1, 2023 must have a thermal efficiency (TE) of not less than 80 percent, and the 81 percent minimum applies only to furnaces manufactured starting on January 1, 2023. The proposal of Step 1 came before that date, so a furnace built that day at the federal minimum has a TE of 80 percent.

Step 3. Source input (Doc 4, Discussion and section II.C): DOE estimated that a furnace with a TE of 81 percent could show a TE2 as low as 77.5 percent, the case of high jacket losses and poor part-load performance. Jacket losses could account for as much as a 2.5 percent difference in efficiency. The estimate rests on the 50 percent weighting of part load that DOE adopted.

Step 4. Calculation (Doc 4): 81 - 77.5 - 2.5 = 1 percentage point, the part of that shortfall due to part-load performance at DOE's weighting. The rest is jacket loss, heat escaping through the cabinet, which does not depend on how part load is weighted.

Step 5. Source input (Doc 4, section II.C): in NEEA's modeling a furnace ran at full load as little as 25 percent of the time and at part load 75 percent of the time, the largest part-load share.

Step 6. Calculation (Doc 4): 75 / 50 = 1.5 percentage points once the part-load shortfall of Step 4 is scaled from DOE's weighting to NEEA's largest part-load share.

Step 7. Calculation (Doc 2 and Doc 4): 80 - 2.5 - 1.5 = 76.0 percent, the lowest TE2 for that furnace: its TE from Step 2 less the jacket losses of Step 3 and the re-weighted part-load shortfall of Step 6.
sections.targeted failure modes:
### Failure mode 1
Trap: Wrong year or edition
How a careless solver fails: Uses the wrong period or date

Why these are traps: Wrong year or edition: Doc 4 dates the TE2 proposal February 25, 2022 and uses the 81 percent minimum in its example, but Doc 2 applies 81 only to furnaces built from January 1, 2023. Taking 81 gives 77.0. With the 80 percent minimum the answer is 76.0.
